extracted.intended_audience: federal judges drafting jury instructions, patent litigators, and juries in U.S. patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions describing the legal elements and factual questions jurors must decide for patent infringement (including §271(f)(2) and §271(g)) and for invalidity defenses (prior art, anticipation, public use, on-sale bar, printed publication, prior invention, etc.). Intended to guide verdict form/jury findings in U.S. patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(2), the plaintiff must prove each of the following more likely than not: (1) the defendant actually supplied the components from the United States into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied from the United States to a foreign country; (2) the defendant knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim of the patent; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) the defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to find that the components actually were combined into an infringing product, only that the defendant intended the components to be combined into a product that would have infringed the patent if combined in the United States. Relevant authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2); WesternGeco v. ION, Microsoft v. AT&T, Cardiac Pacemakers v. St. Jude, Waymark v. Porta Sys., Rotec v. Mitsubishi. (Use these elements when instructing the jury.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by import/sale/offer/use of product made by a patented process (35 U.S.C. § 271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under Section 271(g), the plaintiff must prove more likely than not that: (1) the defendant imported into the United States or, within the United States, sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the patent; (2) the product was made between the patent's issue date and its expiration (or the date of trial, as applicable); and (3) the defendant imported/sold/offered/used the product between those dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must decide whether the evidence establishes the product was “made by” the claimed process. Do not find “made by” if the product was materially changed by later processes or if the product is only a trivial or non-essential part of another product. Infringement under §271(g) does not require a single entity to perform all process steps. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 271(g); Syngenta v. Wildwood; Amgen v. Roche; others. (Include dates and claim references in the instruction.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant’s burden to prove invalidity (clear and convincing evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This burden never changes regardless of whether a prior art reference was considered during prosecution. Practice note: if the PTO did not have all material facts, the challenger’s burden may be easier to sustain and it may be appropriate to instruct the jury to evaluate whether evidence is materially new and consider that when determining whether invalidity is proven by clear and convincing evidence. Authorities: Microsoft v. i4i; Sciele Pharma v. Lupin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (pre-AIA) — what counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes items received into evidence showing: (a) any product or method publicly known or used by others in the United States before the claimed invention was invented; (b) any product or method that was in public use or on sale in the United States before the Cutoff Date; (c) any patents that issued before the Cutoff Date; (d) any publications with dates of public accessibility before the Cutoff Date; and (e) any product or method that was made by anyone in the United States before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the particular prior art references admitted into evidence. Cite 35 U.S.C. § 102 (pre-AIA) and relevant case law. (If parties dispute status/date/public availability, instruct the jury on those factual issues.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (AIA) — what counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes anything patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public anywhere in the world before the effective filing date of the claim; and anything described in a patent or published patent application naming another inventor and filed before the effective filing date of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify particular prior art references admitted into evidence. Cite 35 U.S.C. § 102 (AIA) and § 100(i) (effective filing date). Note exceptions and identify any factual disputes for the jury (e.g., date, public availability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to prior art (one-year disclosures, disclosure-from-inventor, common ownership)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain disclosures made one year or less before the effective filing date are not prior art if: (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or someone who obtained the subject matter from the inventor; or (B) the subject matter had previously been publicly disclosed by the inventor or someone who obtained it from the inventor. Additional exceptions apply where subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation to assign to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions mirror §102(b)/(c) rules; instruct the jury regarding any factual issues about the origin of a disclosure or ownership. Cite Leahy-Smith AIA and Helsinn decisions as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of whether PTO considered a reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a particular prior art reference was considered by the Patent Examiner, the defendant must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice note: If the PTO lacked material facts, it may be easier for the challenger to meet the burden. When requested, consider giving an instruction about the effect of new evidence and whether the evidence is materially new compared to what the PTO had (Microsoft v. i4i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of independent vs dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims stand alone and do not refer to other claims; dependent claims refer to and include all elements of the claim(s) to which they refer plus additional elements. The jury must evaluate invalidity on a claim-by-claim basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims are not automatically invalid — evaluate separately. However, if you find a dependent claim is invalid, then you must find the independent claim from which it depends is also invalid. Provide examples identifying differences between specific independent and dependent claims. Citations: Comaper v. Antec, Callaway v. Acushnet, Ormco v. Align Tech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) for invalidity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the time of the invention or the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct the jury on how to characterize the POSITA (education, experience, typical skills) because that perspective governs what the POSITA would understand from prior art when assessing anticipation or obviousness. Cite 35 U.S.C. § 103; KSR; Continental Can v. Monsanto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove anticipation, the defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention is not new because each element in the claim is present in a single prior art item and arranged/combined in the same way as recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation. In determining whether elements are present, consider what a POSITA would have understood from reviewing the particular prior art reference. If parties dispute whether an item is prior art, instruct accordingly. Cite numerous Fed. Cir. authorities and practice notes on inherency where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference inherently anticipates if missing elements or features necessarily result from what the single item teaches; to prove inherent anticipation, the party must prove the allegedly inherent features necessarily existed by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence outside the prior art reference (including experimental testing) may be used to show inherency. It is not sufficient that the elements were likely to have existed; they must necessarily have existed or resulted. The fact that elements were unrecognized at the time does not prevent inherency if they necessarily were present. Provide an instruction on inherency when alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention defined in the claim was publicly known by others in the United States before the invention by the patentee (pre-AIA §102(a) context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a factual dispute about date of invention or priority date, instruct the jury on how to determine cutoff dates. Cite pre-AIA statutory sections and relevant cases (e.g., Minn. Mining v. Chemque, Woodland Trust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA, a claim is invalid if the claimed invention was available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual disputes involve disclosures made within one year of the effective filing date or disclosures obtained from the inventor, include instruction on §102(b)/(c) exceptions. Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) and relevant practice notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (pre-AIA) — definition and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was publicly used by others in the United States before the relevant cutoff date. A public use requires (1) accessibility to the public or commercial exploitation in the U.S., and (2) readiness for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factors: nature of public activity, public access, confidentiality obligations on observers, commercial exploitation (even if specifics kept secret), testing/experimentation circumstances, absence of concealment. Secret use by a third party is not public unless public or employees had access. If pre-AIA §102(b) is at issue, instruct that readiness for patenting requires reduction to practice or sufficiently detailed drawings/descriptions enabling a POSITA to make or use the invention. Cite Pfaff, Barry v. Medtronic, Clock Spring, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (AIA) — worldwide public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA, a claim is invalid if the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors similar to pre-AIA public use apply (public access, confidentiality, testing circumstances). Commercial exploitation anywhere in the world may qualify even if the specifics of the invention were kept secret. Invention must also have been ready for patenting (reduction to practice or adequate descriptions). Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) and practice notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if, before the applicable cutoff date, an embodiment of the claimed invention was (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (pre-AIA limited to the U.S. for some rules), and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commercial offer for sale exists if another party could form a binding contract by accepting the offer. An invention may be subject to an offer for sale even if done confidentially; sale is not required nor is disclosure of invention details. Readiness for patenting requires reduction to practice or sufficiently specific drawings/descriptions to enable a POSITA. Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(b) (pre-AIA) and §102(a)(1) (AIA), Pfaff, Helsinn, Medicines Co., and other authorities. Include practice-note details when factual issues arise about one-year disclosures or ownership exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain prior uses or sales may not be treated as public use or placing the invention on sale if the primary purpose was legitimate experimentation by or under the control of the inventor (or assignee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentation must relate to claimed features and be for technological improvement (not primarily commercial). Third-party experimentation for its own purposes does not qualify. Incidental profit is permissible if experimentation is primary. A test done primarily for marketing is not experimental. If defendant shows prior public use/sale by clear and convincing evidence, burden shifts to plaintiff to show experimental purpose; strong evidence of experimental use may negate the defendant’s showing. Cite City of Elizabeth v. Nicholson Pavement, Barry v. Medtronic, Polara Eng’g, Clock Spring, and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a printed publication (maintained in tangible form) that was sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter before the relevant cutoff date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Printed publication’ includes printed pages, electronic files, microfilm, photographs, internet publications, photocopies, issued patents, and published patent applications as of their publication date. Accessibility means persons interested and ordinarily skilled exercising reasonable diligence could locate it. The disclosure must be enabling (complete enough to enable a POSITA to use the invention without undue experimentation). Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(a)/(b) (pre-AIA) and §§102(a)(1)/(a)(2) (AIA), and related cases. Include practice-note instruction on accessibility when disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior invention (pre-AIA) — earlier inventor by others in U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee (pre-AIA §102(a)/(g) context). The defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) the third party reduced to practice a product/method with all claim features before the patentee’s invention, or (2) the third party conceived first and exercised reasonable diligence to later reduce to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defendant must also prove the prior product/method was sufficiently developed that a POSITA would recognize it would work for its intended purpose. The defense may be negated if the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If priority of invention is submitted to the jury additional instructions on conception, reduction to practice, and diligence are required. Cite Teva v. AstraZeneca, Rosco v. Mirror Lite, Dow Chem. v. Astro-Valcour, and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment, suppression, or concealment of a prior invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior invention does not anticipate the patent if it was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed by the prior inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may find abandonment/suppression/concealment if there is clear and convincing evidence the prior inventor actively concealed the invention or unreasonably delayed making it public. Generally a prior invention was not abandoned/suppressed/concealed if it was publicly made, sold, offered for sale, or otherwise used commercially. Periods of delay do not necessarily constitute abandonment if the prior inventor engaged in reasonable efforts to bring the invention to market. Provide definitions and examples if the issue is asserted. Cite Dow Chem. v. Astro-Valcour, Checkpoint Sys. v. USITC, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent as prior art (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was disclosed in a prior patent issued before the applicable cutoff date (pre-AIA context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anticipation or obviousness is based on a prior filing date (e.g., earlier-filed patent application), use the specific instructions addressing prior-filed applications and effective filing dates (see Section 6.8 cross-reference). Provide factual identification of the prior patent(s) admitted into evidence and relevant dates.
